FOR MOBILE BRIDAL HAIR & MAKEUP ARTISTS

Can one artist finish this bridal party on time — and what does the booking actually total?

A rate card with one row per service can't tell you whether the group fits your schedule before the ceremony, or how much crediting a trial fee is quietly discounting the booking. This free calculator prices every person, tops up to your minimum, checks the schedule against the artists you've booked, and reports one total. Nothing you type leaves your browser.

A planning figure from the numbers you typed, not an audited statement or a contract. It does not add sales tax you collect and remit, income tax, or product cost per client unless you fold those into your prices yourself.

Private by default

Everything on this page runs in your browser. Your prices, headcounts, and fees are never uploaded, there is no account, and nothing is saved when you close the tab. Copy shareable link is the one way these figures leave this device, and only because you choose to send them: they ride in the page's URL fragment, which a browser never puts in a request line or a Referer header. Whoever holds that link can read the numbers in it, so send it the way you would send the numbers themselves. We count only anonymous local feature events (booking-priced, assistant-needed, link_copied) so we can tell whether the calculator gets used — no prices, headcounts, or client details are recorded, and Do Not Track / Global Privacy Control turn it off automatically.

Common questions

Does crediting the trial fee toward the wedding day cost me money?

Yes, and that is easy to miss. "Your trial fee comes off your wedding day total if you book" reads as goodwill, but it lowers the combined amount you collect across both bookings by up to the trial fee itself — the same booking is worth less to you than the identical booking without that policy. This calculator shows the total contract value both ways so the discount is a number you chose rather than one that fell out of a rate card nobody added up.

How do I know if I need a second artist?

Add up every person's service minutes plus a buffer for setup and product changes, then compare that to the minutes available from arrival to the moment the bride has to be dressed, multiplied by the artists already booked. If the group needs more minutes than that window has, one artist cannot finish everyone on time no matter how early they start within the window — the fix is an additional artist, not a faster pace. The calculator runs this check and reports exactly how many more artists the schedule needs.

Why does the bride get extra minutes on top of the bridal-party rate?

A bride's look is typically more detailed and often includes a final check right before photos, so it takes longer than the identical service on a bridal-party member. Pricing the bride separately from the party, and scheduling extra minutes for her specifically, keeps both the price and the timeline honest about that difference instead of averaging it away.

What is the point of a dollar service minimum if I also have a headcount minimum?

They answer different questions. A headcount minimum is about whether a small booking is worth the morning's commitment at all, regardless of price. A dollar minimum is the enforceable floor once you have decided to take it — it tops up a small or heavily-discounted booking to a total that still covers your time and travel, rather than declining it outright.

Does anything about my clients or my prices get uploaded?

No. Every field on this page runs in your browser only, there is no account, and nothing you type is uploaded. Nothing leaves this device unless you choose to send it: the Copy shareable link button puts the figures on the form into the page's URL fragment, which a browser never sends to a server or into a Referer header, so it reaches only the person you hand the link to. Anyone who has that link can read the numbers in it, so send it the way you would send the numbers themselves. Usage counting only tallies anonymous feature events, and you can turn it off with the button above.

Curious how this compares to charging one flat day rate for the whole bridal party? Read this calculator vs. a flat day rate. Already running your client pipeline through HoneyBook? Read this calculator vs. HoneyBook. Wondering how a big bridal party can price fine and still not fit your morning? Read why a priced booking can still be impossible to finish.

This calculator vs. a flat day rate

A flat day rate — one lump sum for the whole bridal party's morning — is the fastest way to quote a wedding, and for a party that is nearly always the same size it can work fine. It stops working the moment the group's size, mix of services, start time, or trial-fee policy varies from booking to booking, because none of that is tracked separately in a single number.

What each one is for

A flat day rate is quick to quote and simple for a client to hear. What it does not do is separate the price into anything an artist can check against a specific booking — it does not scale automatically with headcount, it has no early-start or travel logic built in, and it cannot tell you whether the group fits inside the time you have before the ceremony.

This calculator prices the bride, the bridal party, hair-only, makeup-only, and kids' services separately, applies an early-start fee and travel, tops a small booking up to your service minimum, and runs the one check a lump sum cannot: whether the artists booked can actually finish everyone on time, and if not, exactly how many more artists the schedule needs.

QuestionWhere to answer it
What do I charge for a typical bridal party?Either one — a flat rate is fine if the size and mix rarely change.
What does an unusually large or small party actually cost?This calculator — it prices the exact headcount and mix, not an average.
Can one artist finish this group before the ceremony?This calculator's schedule check, not a flat rate — a lump sum tracks no minutes at all.
What does crediting a trial fee actually cost me?This calculator's total contract value, computed both ways instead of worked out by hand.
Is anything I enter uploaded anywhere?No. The calculator runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent to a server.

Common questions

What is a flat day rate, and why do artists use it?

One lump sum for the whole bridal party's morning, regardless of exactly who gets what service. It is fast to quote and easy for a client to understand, which is why many artists start with it — especially for a bridal party that is usually about the same size.

What does a flat rate hide as the group gets bigger or smaller?

The price stays the same while the work does not. A flat rate sized for four bridesmaids under-prices an eight-person party and over-prices a two-person one, and it says nothing about whether one artist can actually finish either group before the ceremony — that is a scheduling question a lump sum cannot answer.

Can a flat rate tell me if I need a second artist?

No. A flat rate is a price, not a schedule. Whether one artist can finish a given group depends on the minutes each service takes, the buffer between clients, and the window from arrival to the must-be-ready deadline — none of which a lump sum quote tracks. A booking can be priced generously and still be physically impossible for one person to finish on time.

Does a flat rate handle a credited trial fee correctly?

Only if the artist works out the interaction by hand every time. Crediting a trial fee toward a flat day-rate booking is still a real discount on the combined total, and a flat quote has no built-in way to show that — it is one more thing tracked on the side rather than computed.

Is anything I enter uploaded anywhere?

No. The calculator this page links to runs entirely in your browser; nothing you enter is uploaded.

No warranty. This page and the linked calculator produce planning estimates from numbers you supply, not a contract or a guarantee of scheduling feasibility. You are responsible for verifying anything here against your own booking and rate card. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Nothing leaves your browser. The calculator this page links to runs entirely client-side; nothing you enter is uploaded anywhere.

Nothing here says or implies that a flat day rate is a bad way to price a wedding — it is a different job: simple to quote where this calculator is detailed where a booking varies.

This calculator vs. HoneyBook

Two different shapes: HoneyBook runs a bridal hair and makeup business's client relationship end to end -- proposal, contract, invoice and payment -- as an ongoing account. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question -- what should this wedding's booking cost, given the bride, bridal party, hair-only, makeup-only and kids' services on it, the early-start fee, mileage, and whether the artists already booked can finish the whole group before the must-be-ready deadline.

What each one is for

HoneyBook is a client management platform widely used by creative and service businesses that book project-based work, and it is well documented as one of the industry-standard tools among bridal hair and makeup artists specifically -- HoneyBook publishes its own "Bridal Hair & Makeup Proposal" and "Bridal Hair & Makeup Pricing Guide" templates for exactly this trade. Its signature feature is a combined proposal-contract-invoice document (its own term is a "smart file") that lets a bride review package options, sign the contract, and pay a deposit in one flow, tied to one account used on an ongoing basis across every client the business books. HoneyBook's own site is not reachable from this session to confirm today's specific plan names or pricing, so only its well-documented identity and category are stated here: nothing about it is invented, and no dollar figure for it appears on this page. Public descriptions of that kind of platform describe building a proposal, collecting a signature and a deposit, and invoicing the remaining balance once a price already exists; none describe pricing the bride, bridal party, hair-only, makeup-only and kids' tiers against an early-start fee and mileage, or checking whether the artists already on the schedule can physically finish the group in time -- which is what this calculator does.

This calculator does none of what HoneyBook does. It does not manage a client pipeline, send a contract, collect a signature, or take a payment. It takes one wedding-day booking's services, prices each tier, applies the early-start fee and mileage, tops a small booking up to a service minimum, credits a trial fee against the wedding-day balance so the discount is visible rather than hidden in the timing, and checks the booked artists' capacity against the must-be-ready deadline -- then reports how many additional artists the schedule needs, if any.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I need to manage my client pipeline, send a proposal and contract, and collect a signature and payment.HoneyBook, or a comparable client management platform -- running that ongoing relationship is not something this calculator does.
What should this wedding's booking cost, given the bridal party size and any early start or mileage?This calculator -- free, instant, private, no account.
Can the artists I've already booked finish the whole group before the ceremony's must-be-ready time?This calculator's schedule-capacity check -- it flags exactly how many more artists the group needs, if any.
Does crediting the trial fee toward the wedding-day balance actually save the client money, or is it just a timing change?This calculator -- it reports the trial credit as the real discount it is, against the combined total.
I already have a price and need to send a proposal, collect a signature, and take a deposit.HoneyBook -- built as an account-based platform for exactly that job.
Do I need to create an account or sign up to use the tool?This calculator: no. HoneyBook's tools are used through a paid account.

Most mobile bridal hair and makeup artists get different value from each: HoneyBook (or a comparable client management platform) for running proposals, contracts and payments across an ongoing client pipeline as an account, and a private calculator like this one for an instant, no-login price and staffing check for one wedding's booking before it goes into a proposal. This page's own figures are a pricing and scheduling model, not a contract or an invoice.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or HoneyBook?

They do different jobs, and a mobile bridal hair and makeup artist may well end up using both. HoneyBook is a client management platform widely used across the wedding industry -- it publishes its own bridal hair and makeup proposal and pricing-guide templates -- built around an account-based "smart file" that combines a proposal, contract and invoice into one document a bride reviews, signs and pays a deposit against. It manages the client relationship on an ongoing basis across every booking a business takes. This calculator does one narrower thing: given the bride, bridal party, hair-only, makeup-only and kids' services on one wedding-day booking, it prices each tier, applies an early-start fee and mileage, tops a small booking up to a service minimum, credits a trial fee against the balance, and checks whether the artists already booked can finish the whole group before the must-be-ready deadline -- flagging exactly how many more artists the schedule needs. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type. An artist already managing an ongoing client pipeline, sending contracts, and collecting payments is better served by HoneyBook or a comparable platform; an artist who wants an instant, private total and staffing check for one wedding's booking is in the right place here.

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by HoneyBook. HoneyBook is a trademark of its owner, named here only to describe what this calculator is and is not.

why-a-priced-booking-can-still-be-imposs.text:
← back to the calculator

Why a booking that prices fine can still be impossible to finish

A rate card answers one question: does this booking clear your revenue minimum? It never answers the other one: can one artist actually finish everyone before the ceremony? Those are independent checks, and a group can pass the first easily while failing the second completely.

A worked example

A bride plus six bridesmaids, all taking the full hair-and-makeup service, at this calculator's own default rates and timings. One artist is booked, with a 4-hour (240-minute) window from arrival to the must-be-ready deadline.

CheckResult
Headcount7 (1 bride + 6 bridesmaids)
Service revenue (before minimums, travel, early start)$1,125.00
Service minimum$500.00 at 3+ people -- cleared with room to spare
Total minutes needed (services + buffers)520 minutes
Minutes available (1 artist × 240-minute window)240 minutes
Minutes short280 minutes
Additional artists needed2 -- three artists total, not one

The revenue check passes by a wide margin -- $1,125 against a $500 minimum, more than double. The schedule check fails just as clearly: 520 minutes of work does not fit in one artist's 240-minute window, no matter what the booking is priced at. This calculator prices the two extra artists into the booking automatically once it detects the shortfall -- $300.00 charged to the client for two assistants, $250.00 paid out to them, a $50.00 markup on the arrangement -- rather than leaving the artist to discover mid-morning that the group cannot be finished on time.

Every figure above comes from this calculator's own default rates and timings, run through the shipped scheduling arithmetic -- nothing here is rounded by hand.

Common questions

How can a booking be priced fine and still be impossible to finish?

Because price and schedule are two separate checks, and a rate card only ever runs the first one. Revenue comes from headcount times each person's price; feasibility comes from the total minutes every service takes, plus a buffer per person, against the minutes actually available before the must-be-ready deadline. A group large enough to clear your revenue minimum easily can still need more total minutes than one artist has hours in the morning.

What actually determines whether one artist can finish a group?

Three numbers: how many minutes each service takes (a full hair-and-makeup look is slower than hair alone), a buffer added after every person for setup and product changes, and the prep window -- the minutes from arrival to the deadline. Multiply minutes-per-service by headcount, add the buffers, and compare the total to the prep window. If the total is higher, one artist cannot finish everyone in time, regardless of how well the booking is priced.

What is the fix when the schedule does not fit?

A second (or third) artist working in parallel, which adds prep-window minutes to the booking's total capacity. That artist is a real cost -- a payout to whoever is booked -- and normally a real line item charged to the client, not something absorbed into the original quote. The gap between what the client is charged for the extra artist and what that artist is paid is the only part of this that is actually a pricing decision; everything upstream of it is a scheduling constraint, not a price.

Does a bigger rate card price prevent this?

No. Raising a service's price changes revenue, not the minutes that service takes to perform. A booking can be priced at any level and still take more total minutes than the prep window allows -- pricing and scheduling are independent, and a rate card that only tracks price has nothing that would catch the second one.
